pages.text: In Ghana, many people use traditional plants for medicine. These plants come from the Ga and Twi tribes. People use them because Western medicine is becoming very expensive.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Ghana Street Market

pages.text: Women pick herbs in the morning and sell them in Accra. They sell leaves, stems, and bark. Many people in Ghana depend on these markets for their health. The Center for Plant Medicine Research helps study these plants.

It was started in 1976. They want to prove that traditional knowledge works using science. About 16,000 patients visit their clinic every month. People in rural areas know which plants to use for sickness.
They use them for malaria or typhoid. It is easy and cheap to find these plants near their homes. Experts say that using the right amount of a plant is very important for safety.

evidence: T he traditional medicine market in Ghana, West Africa, is thriving, offering countless cures passed down by generations of Indigenous Ga and Twi tribes.
The Center for Plant Medicine Research , created by the Ghanaian government in 1976, works with raw plant material to create natural products and treat patients.
Their outpatient clinic sees roughly 16,000 patients a month.
A1-A2.headline: Ghana Plants Offer Another Way to Heal

pages.text: The traditional medicine market in Ghana is currently thriving as citizens seek alternatives to rising costs for Western pharmaceuticals. For generations, Indigenous Ga and Twi tribes have passed down knowledge regarding the healing properties of local flora. Today, this practice remains a vital component of the national healthcare system.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Ghana Street Market

pages.text: In rural Ghana, women harvest medicinal herbs from the bush and cultivated plots to sell in Accra. These markets provide fresh vines, leaves, and bark to a large portion of the population. According to a 2023 study in Frontiers in Pharmacology, approximately 60 to 70 percent of Ghanaians rely on these traditional markets for their medical needs.

The Center for Plant Medicine Research, established in 1976, plays a crucial role in validating this traditional knowledge through scientific methods. Dr. Kofi Donkor, the deputy director, emphasizes that practitioners possess deep professional expertise passed down through families. The center’s clinic treats roughly 16,000 patients monthly, highlighting the demand for natural alternatives.

For rural villagers, accessibility, cost, and familiarity make plant-based medicine a practical choice. Many residents can identify plants to treat common ailments like malaria or typhoid without needing a practitioner. While these remedies offer a sustainable path toward universal health care, experts caution that proper dosage remains essential for effective and safe treatment.

evidence: As prices for Western pharmaceuticals and Western medical care rise, Ghanaians are relying on the medical remedies they have always turned to: plants.

B1-B2.headline: Plants offer Ghanaians a medicine alternative

pages.text: The traditional medicine sector in Ghana is experiencing a significant resurgence, driven by the escalating costs of Western medical care and pharmaceuticals. Indigenous knowledge, preserved by the Ga and Twi tribes, serves as the foundation for a healthcare model that remains deeply integrated into the daily lives of most Ghanaians. This reliance on botanical remedies is not merely a cultural preference but a pragmatic response to economic pressures.
pages.caption: Illustrative image: Ghana Street Market

pages.text: The Center for Plant Medicine Research, founded in 1976, acts as a bridge between ancestral wisdom and modern clinical science. Dr. Kofi Donkor, the deputy director, notes that the center’s primary objective is to validate traditional knowledge through rigorous scientific inquiry. By analyzing raw plant materials, the center provides a scientific framework for practices that have been passed down through generations. Their outpatient facility, which serves roughly 16,000 patients monthly, underscores the efficacy and public trust in these natural treatments.

In rural regions, the proximity to forests and meadows allows villagers to utilize local flora for primary healthcare. A 2023 study in Frontiers in Pharmacology indicates that 60 to 70 percent of the population depends on these traditional markets. Furthermore, data suggests that in many developing nations, traditional medicine accounts for 80 percent of primary healthcare, significantly contributing to universal health goals.

Despite the benefits, experts emphasize the importance of precision in dosage. While many rural residents possess the expertise to treat common ailments, the role of the traditional practitioner remains vital for complex conditions. As researchers continue to investigate plants like croton membranaceous for potential cancer treatments, the integration of Indigenous knowledge into the formal medical landscape offers a sustainable and accessible future for healthcare in West Africa.

evidence: The deep green forests and meadows of rural Ghana have been home to rural villagers for many years, so many villagers are already familiar with the various plants that can heal a disease.
Living near these forests makes plant-based medicine an easy, cheaper option for treating disease in rural Ghana, when Western pharmacies are too expensive or far away.
It is the knowledge from the practitioners that we try to validate using scientific methods.

title: How Croatian communities are taking on planned poultry slaughterhouses
sourceTitle: How Croatian communities are taking on planned poultry slaughterhouses
headline: Croatian communities fight slaughterhouse plans
attribution: Global Voices — original reporting; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Sisak is a city in Croatia. It is famous for its oil refinery. Now, it is in the news because of chickens. Companies want to build big poultry farms there. Many people do not want these farms. They say the farms will hurt the environment and the animals.
pages.caption: A chicken. Photo by David Goehring, CC BY 2.0.

imageProvenance.credit: A chicken. Photo by David Goehring via Flickr,

pages.text: By April 2026, there were 24 planned projects. Two big companies are behind them. One is MHP and the other is Premium Chicken Company. These companies want to make a lot of money. They plan to send most of the chicken to other countries. People are very angry.
pages.caption: Sunset in Sisak.

imageProvenance.credit: Sunset in Sisak. Photo by Aktron via Wikimedia Commons,

pages.text: In February, 5,000 people protested in Zagreb. Later, 1,000 people protested in Sisak. Over 51,000 people signed a petition. They are worried about pollution in the Kupa and Sava rivers. Actor Goran Višnjić also asked people to help stop the projects. In a small village called Apatija, people are also fighting.

They say the farm will destroy their home. They worry about 6,500 tons of manure and 60 million liters of wastewater. The mayor says the farms are good for the economy, but the people disagree. MHP stopped one project in May 2026 because the community said no. However, other projects are still moving forward.

evidence: Sisak, a city known for its manufacturing industry and for operating the second largest oil refinery in Croatia, has been receiving an unusual amount of media coverage about chickens.
The first major national protest back in February saw around 5,000 people take to the streets in Zagreb, according to organizers .
“We don’t want to become an industrial village […] Apatija has no sewage system; where will 6,500 tons of manure and 60 million liters of wastewater go?” asks resident Marko Denačić.
A1-A2.headline: Croatian Towns Oppose New Poultry Plants

pages.text: Citizens in Sisak, Croatia, are actively opposing a series of industrial poultry facilities proposed for their region. The city, historically recognized for its manufacturing and oil refinery, has become the center of a national debate regarding environmental standards and animal welfare. By April 2026, organizers identified 24 planned poultry projects across three counties, led by major investors including the agricultural conglomerate MHP and the Premium Chicken Company (PCC).
pages.caption: A chicken. Photo by David Goehring, CC BY 2.0.

imageProvenance.credit: A chicken. Photo by David Goehring via Flickr,

pages.text: Public opposition has been significant. A major protest in February drew 5,000 participants in Zagreb, followed by a demonstration of 1,000 people in Sisak. Over 51,000 citizens signed a petition citing concerns over transparency and potential environmental damage. Actor Goran Višnjić publicly supported the movement, warning that the projects threaten the Kupa and Sava rivers and could lead to the closure of 250 domestic farms.
pages.caption: Sunset in Sisak.

imageProvenance.credit: Sunset in Sisak. Photo by Aktron via Wikimedia Commons,

pages.text: In the village of Apatija, residents formed the Apatija Civic Initiative to challenge a facility planned just 400 meters from their homes. Resident Marko Denačić highlighted the lack of infrastructure, questioning how the area would manage 6,500 tons of manure and 60 million liters of wastewater. While local officials like Mayor Dubravko Bilić argue these projects are essential for economic growth, the community remains skeptical.

The pressure has yielded some results. In May 2026, MHP withdrew from its Sisak-area project due to a lack of local support, which canceled 12 of the 24 planned subprojects. However, PCC continues to pursue its remaining developments, leaving activists to demand stronger government oversight and a review of all environmental impact assessments.

evidence: Over 51,000 people signed a petition to voice their opposition, for reasons ranging from the state’s lack of transparency regarding environmental assessments to allegations of favoritism towards specific investors.
“We’ll be left with pollution, stench, destroyed nature, and the shutdown of around 250 domestic farms,” said Višnjić.

According to Greenpeace International , local authorities subsequently confirmed that MHP’s withdrawal canceled 12 of the 24 Sisak-Moslavina county subprojects, while PCC continued to pursue the remaining 12.
B1-B2.headline: Croatian communities fight slaughterhouse plans

pages.text: The industrial landscape of Sisak, Croatia, is currently the focal point of a contentious struggle between local communities and large-scale agricultural investors. Sisak, traditionally defined by its oil refinery and manufacturing heritage, has seen an influx of media attention following the proposal of numerous industrial poultry facilities. By April 2026, activists had cataloged 24 distinct projects across three counties, spearheaded by the agricultural conglomerate MHP and the Premium Chicken Company (PCC).
pages.caption: A chicken. Photo by David Goehring, CC BY 2.0.

imageProvenance.credit: A chicken. Photo by David Goehring via Flickr,

pages.text: These proposals have sparked widespread alarm regarding the potential for environmental degradation, the erosion of local living standards, and the ethical implications of intensive animal farming. The scale of public resistance is unprecedented, with a February protest in Zagreb attracting 5,000 participants and a subsequent rally in Sisak drawing over 1,000. Supported by 160 civil society organizations, including Greenpeace, the movement has garnered over 51,000 signatures on a petition demanding greater transparency in environmental assessments.
pages.caption: Sunset in Sisak.

imageProvenance.credit: Sunset in Sisak. Photo by Aktron via Wikimedia Commons,

pages.text: High-profile figures, such as actor Goran Višnjić, have amplified these concerns, specifically warning of the ecological risks to the Kupa and Sava rivers and the potential displacement of 250 domestic farms. In the village of Apatija, the local civic initiative has mounted a robust campaign against a facility slated for construction within 400 meters of residential areas.

Residents have raised critical questions regarding the management of 6,500 tons of manure and 60 million liters of wastewater in a region lacking adequate sewage infrastructure. Despite the dismissive stance of local officials like Mayor Dubravko Bilić, who frames these investments as vital for economic development, the community remains steadfast in its opposition. The collective resistance has achieved tangible outcomes.

In May 2026, MHP announced its withdrawal from the Sisak-area project, citing a lack of community support, which effectively terminated 12 of the 24 planned subprojects. Nevertheless, PCC persists with its remaining 12 proposals, prompting activists to call for a comprehensive review of all environmental impact assessments and a reevaluation of the state's investment priorities. The ongoing conflict underscores a broader tension between industrial expansion and the preservation of local agricultural dynamics.

evidence: By April 2026, protest organizers said they had identified 24 planned poultry projects across three Croatian counties , being advanced separately by two investors: agricultural conglomerate MHP (formerly Myronivsky Hliboprodukt), one of the largest poultry companies in Europe, and Premium Chicken Company (PCC), owned by the Croatian holding company Renaissance Capital d.o.o. (LLC), not to be confused with the similarly named Moscow-based investment bank Renaissance Capital (RenCap).
More than 1,000 people attended a follow-up protest in Sisak a couple of months later, backed by over 160 civil society organizations, including Friends of the Earth Europe and Greenpeace .
Speaking in an Instagram reel , Višnjić urged citizens to join the February 21 protest and warned of the threats to the ecosystem, including both the Kupa and Sava rivers.
